articles.title: Christmas lights switch-ons 2026: dates and times for Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Norden
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton switch on this Saturday 14 November, Shawclough on Thursday 19 November, Rochdale and Norden on Sunday 22 November and Littleborough on Saturday 28 November.
articles.content_html:
Christmas lights will be switched on in Heywood and Middleton this Saturday, with Shawclough, Rochdale, Norden and Littleborough following over the next two weeks.

The dates are Saturday 14 November for Heywood and Middleton, Thursday 19 November for Shawclough, Sunday 22 November for Rochdale town centre and Norden, and Saturday 28 November for Littleborough.

All six events are free. Road closures and parking restrictions apply around the five weekend events.

Heywood, Saturday 14 November: the Heywood Christmas Festival takes place in the town centre. Rochdale Borough Council's traffic notice says road closures will be in place from 10am until 6pm, and waiting is banned along the whole of Bethel Street.

A funding report to Heywood Township in the summer proposed a day of family entertainment and fireworks for the switch-on. The switch-on time was not given in the notices seen by Rochdale Daily.

Middleton, Saturday 14 November: the switch-on event is in Middleton Gardens and starts at 12pm, according to the Rochdale Times. It includes food and drink stalls, fairground rides and market stalls, among them the Teenage Market for young traders.

The Art House is hosting Christmas card-making and face painting for children. Middleton Brass Band plays at 4.30pm, before the lights are switched on.

Shawclough, Thursday 19 November: the Shawclough Christmas lights switch-on takes place at Syke Community Base.

A Christmas tree is also planned at the soldier memorial, known locally as "the soldier", opposite the Healey Hotel. The switch-on time has not yet been announced.

Rochdale town centre, Sunday 22 November: Father Christmas and the Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, will switch on the lights at around 5.30pm in front of Rochdale Town Hall, according to the council.

The switch-on is the final night of the Ignite Fire Festival, which runs from 5pm to 8pm on Friday 20, Saturday 21 and Sunday 22 November in the square and gardens around the town hall, including Broadfield Slopes. Entry is free.

This year's centrepiece is BODY, a night-time trail by outdoor arts company Walk the Plank. The council says it takes visitors through six zones of the human body using fire, light, sound and special effects.

Organisers warn that Ignite includes flashing lights, fire effects, loud noises, smoke and pyrotechnics.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, said: "Ignite is the perfect way to kick off the festive season, bringing together spectacular entertainment, dazzling displays and magical moments for all ages."

Norden, Sunday 22 November: the Norden Christmas lights event is on the same day as the Rochdale switch-on. The council's traffic notice says roads will be closed for the event, with no loading or waiting and no signed alternative route for vehicles. Drivers should check the notice on the council's website for the roads and times.

Littleborough, Saturday 28 November: Church Street will be closed from 1.30pm until 7pm for the Littleborough Christmas Lights Event, according to the council's traffic notice. Waiting is banned from noon until 7pm. The notice does not give the switch-on time.

Later in the season, the borough's Christmas Toy Appeal is collecting new, unwrapped gifts at libraries and leisure centres until Friday 11 December.

Heywood Civic's pantomime this year is Aladdin, and Cinderella opens at Middleton Arena on Sunday 20 December.

At Rochdale Town Hall, Brass and Bublé: A Christmas Special is on Sunday 13 December at 7.15pm, and Jonathan Scott's Christmas organ concert is on Wednesday 16 December.

Rochdale Daily will update this guide as organisers confirm switch-on times.

Sources: Rochdale Borough Council, Rochdale Town Hall, Visit Rochdale and the Rochdale Times; Shawclough details supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: Rochdale Borough Council.

articles.title: Rochdale to face York City again after April title decider
articles.excerpt: Rochdale will meet York City in League Two, marking their first encounter since last season's thrilling title decider in the National League.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale will face York City in League Two on Saturday at Crown Oil Arena, marking their first meeting since last season's dramatic title decider on 25 April.

In that final match, Rochdale and York City played to a thrilling 1-1 draw, with York clinching automatic promotion thanks to a last-minute equaliser from Josh Stones.

The two clubs finished the season with a remarkable total of 212 points combined, showcasing their competitive spirit in the league.

Both teams have seen changes in their squads and strategies as they adapt to the challenges of League Two.

Rochdale secured their promotion through a tough play-off campaign, while York City managed to secure their place at the top of the National League in dramatic fashion.

This season, both clubs are looking to establish themselves in the English Football League (EFL) and improve their standings.

The outcome of this match could have significant implications for both teams as they continue to establish themselves in League Two, with fans eager to see how both clubs perform after their previous successes.

articles.title: Measles: the symptoms to look out for in your child, and when to get help
articles.excerpt: More than 1,000 measles cases have been confirmed in England this year, 111 of them in the North West. Here is how the illness starts and the warning signs that need urgent care.
articles.content_html:
Parents in Rochdale borough are being reminded what measles looks like, after 1,030 confirmed cases in England between 1 January and 12 October this year.

The North West accounted for 111 of those cases, about 11% of the national total, according to UK Health Security Agency figures.

Two measles-related deaths were confirmed in England earlier this year, both of them children, the agency said in June.

Measles usually starts like a cold, the NHS says. Early signs are a high temperature, a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, a cough, and red, sore, watery eyes.

A few days later, small white spots can appear inside the cheeks and on the back of the lips.

A rash follows a few days after the cold-like symptoms. It starts on the face and behind the ears before spreading over the body, and is usually not itchy.

On white skin the rash looks brown or red. On brown and black skin it can be harder to see.

People with measles are infectious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after it appears.

The NHS advises getting an urgent GP appointment or calling 111 if your child may have measles, has a high temperature that does not come down with paracetamol or ibuprofen, is struggling to breathe, or is feeding or weeing less than usual.

Parents should also seek urgent advice if a baby under one has been in contact with measles.

Ring the GP surgery before going in, so staff can arrange a phone appointment or see your child away from other patients.

Call 999 or go to A&E if someone with measles has a seizure, has severe difficulty breathing, cannot stay awake, is limp or floppy, has a stiff neck, or has a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.

Measles is unlikely in anyone who has had both doses of the MMR or MMRV vaccine, or who has had measles before. Parents unsure whether their child is fully vaccinated can ask their GP surgery, which can give missed doses free on the NHS.

Sources: NHS; UK Health Security Agency. Photograph: Rochdale Daily library.

articles.title: Rochdale IT provider offers solutions for email disruptions during Microsoft outages
articles.excerpt: Rochdale-based IT provider No Fuss IT has urged local businesses to consider alternative communication methods in light of recent Microsoft 365 outages that disrupted email services. The company, led by Finn O’Loughlin, highlighted the potential consequences of email disruptions, including unanswered customer inquiries and delayed purchase orders.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-based IT provider No Fuss IT has urged local businesses to consider alternative communication methods due to recent disruptions in Microsoft 365 email services. The company is encouraging businesses to think about how they would maintain communication if their usual email service became unavailable.

Finn O’Loughlin, who leads the IT team at No Fuss IT, explained that when email services fail, the impact can extend beyond just an empty inbox. He noted that unanswered customer inquiries and delayed purchase orders can significantly disrupt business operations.

"When email stops working, the consequences can reach much further than an empty inbox," O’Loughlin said. "Knowing that someone is working to reopen it does little to move the queue."

No Fuss IT offers email continuity solutions as part of its proactive support services, particularly for organizations working towards or maintaining ISO 9001 and ISO 27001 standards.

This approach is designed to help businesses avoid the pitfalls of email outages, ensuring that communication channels remain open even during technical disruptions.

The recent Microsoft 365 outage has prompted many businesses to reassess their email strategies. O’Loughlin likened the situation to a motorway with an alternative toll road, stating that while the main route is usually reliable, having a backup plan is essential when disruptions occur.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Rochdale IT provider explains how an alternative route can keep business email moving during Microsoft outages | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch Rochdale IT provider explains how an alternative route can keep business email moving during Microsoft outages David Murphy News Editor November 13, 2026 | 10:38 AM Print Microsoft Outlook outage Microsoft 365 disruption has prompted Rochdale-based award-winning IT provider, No Fuss IT, to encourage businesses to look beyond everyday technical support and consider how they would keep communicating if their usual email service became unavailable. No Fuss IT, whose IT team is led by Finn O’Loughlin, provides email continuity as part of its enhanced approach to proactively supporting businesses, including organisations working towards or maintaining ISO 9001 and ISO 27001 requirements. When email stops working, the consequences can reach much further than an empty inbox. Customer enquiries can go unanswered. Purchase orders can be delayed. Staff can lose access to conversations they need to complete their work, while managers spend time finding out what is happening and deciding what to do next. For businesses affected by the latest Microsoft disruption over the last 24 hours, it raises a practical question. If the main route into your email becomes unavailable, have you got another way through? Think of it like a motorway with an alternative toll road. Most days, the motorway gets everyone where they need to go. It is familiar, convenient and part of the daily routine. But when a major incident closes the carriageway, everyone relying on that same route can find themselves stuck. Knowing that someone is working to reopen it does little to move the queue. An alternative toll road offers another route around the blockage. It has a cost, but that cost needs to be considered alongside the time and disruption of sitting still. Email continuity works on a similar principle. Microsoft 365 remains the normal route for everyday email. A separately provided continuity service offers another way to send and receive messages when access to Microsoft’s email service is disrupted. It does not repair Microsoft’s infrastructure. It gives a business an alternative route for its email while the underlying problem is being resolved. A diversion works best when it is planned before the traffic stops. Depending on the agreed service and configuration, staff can use an alternative web portal or supported application to continue communicating. Access to retained messages can help them pick up existing conversations, rather than starting again without the information they need. When normal service returns, synchronisation brings messages handled during the interruption back into the usual email environment. That preparation matters. Staff need to know where to go, how to sign in and who to contact. Administrators need clear procedures for activating continuity and returning to normal operation. Buying a service is one part of the answer. Making sure people can use it when required is another. Proactive support starts before the support ticket. For No Fuss IT, the aim is to make those conversations part of the customer relationship for those wanting to go the extra mile. That means understanding how a business operates, which communications it depends on and what an interruption would prevent its staff from doing. A company processing urgent orders may have different priorities from a professional services firm waiting for client instructions. Both need a plan that reflects their work. Regular conversations help identify those differences and give customers a clearer understanding of what their IT support includes, where the dependencies are and which additional protections would be useful. It also means having a discussion about resilience while everything is working, when there is time to make considered decisions. “Microsoft is working on it” may be an accurate update. It is a rather limited business continuity plan. Keeping communication available also supports sensible cyber security decisions. When normal systems become unavailable, staff may be tempted to move business conversations into personal email accounts or other unapproved channels. Planning an approved alternative helps reduce that pressure. It gives employees a defined way to keep communicating, supported by guidance about access, security and handling business information. No Fuss IT’s approach brings those continuity conversations into its wider cyber security relationships with customers. The purpose is to help businesses understand how availability, secure working practices and day-to-day support fit together. For organisations maintaining ISO 9001 and ISO 27001 management systems, those discussions can support the identification of operational dependencies and relevant risks. Documented arrangements, appropriate controls, testing and reviews remain essential. A continuity product alone does not establish compliance. The motorway comparison has its limits. Email continuity will not restore Teams, SharePoint or every other application affected by a wider Microsoft incident. Its role is specific and valuable, providing another route for business email when the normal one is disrupted. No Fuss IT encourages businesses to establish that route before they need it. articles.title: Rochdale Christmas Toy Appeal aims to deliver 10,000 gifts to children in need
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council's Christmas Toy Appeal seeks donations to provide gifts for 3,000 children living in poverty this festive season.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched its Christmas Toy Appeal, aiming to deliver 10,000 new, unwrapped gifts to 3,000 children living in poverty this festive season.

The appeal, which has been running for 13 years, encourages residents to donate toys to help ensure that no child goes without a present this Christmas.

Donations can be made at various collection points across the borough, including The Trade Centre UK and The Old Police Station. All contributions, regardless of size, are welcomed, with postal deliveries required by 11 December.

The Christmas Toy Appeal has been providing festive cheer to local families since 2013, helping to alleviate some of the pressures faced by those in need during the holiday season.

The council's charity is coordinating the initiative, which has become a vital resource for families in the area.

Residents are encouraged to participate in the appeal to help spread joy and support children in their community. For those wishing to donate, collection points are available throughout Rochdale, and all gifts must be new and unwrapped.

articles.content_html:
A man was seriously injured in an attack on Boundary Street in Rochdale on 8 November 2026. The incident occurred near Stoneyfield Park at approximately 7:50pm, prompting a police investigation into the circumstances surrounding the assault.

Authorities believe the male victim suffered serious injuries during the incident. Greater Manchester Police are currently appealing for witnesses who may have seen or heard anything unusual in the area at the time of the attack.

No further details about the incident have been released by the police. Investigators are working to gather more information and identify any potential suspects involved in the assault.

articles.title: New handmade lock gates installed at Rochdale Canal in Manchester
articles.excerpt: Handcrafted oak gates have been craned into place at Lock 80 on the Rochdale Canal, replacing gates over 25 years old.
articles.content_html:
New handmade oak gates have been craned into place at Lock 80 on the Rochdale Canal, marking a significant upgrade to the historical waterway. The gates, crafted in Yorkshire, weigh between 1,500 kg and 2,500 kg each and replace those installed over 25 years ago.

This installation is part of a broader initiative by the Canal and River Trust to restore lock gates across Greater Manchester's canal network. The project is crucial for maintaining the functionality of the canals, which are vital for local transport and recreation.

A spokesperson for the Canal and River Trust stated, "The new locks are critical to keeping canals open," highlighting the importance of this restoration work.

This project is one of hundreds planned over the next five months to maintain the 2,000-mile canal network across England and Wales.

The Rochdale Canal, which opened in 1804, is one of the first trans-Pennine canals, connecting Manchester to Sowerby Bridge in West Yorkshire. The recent installation follows similar work completed in February 2026 in Manchester's Gay Village, demonstrating ongoing efforts to preserve the region's waterways.

articles.title: Prime Minister Andy Burnham supports reinstatement of Heywood express bus service
articles.excerpt: Andy Burnham backs calls for the return of the 167 bus service from Heywood to Manchester, which was cut in 2012.
articles.content_html:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has backed calls for the reinstatement of the 167 express bus service from Heywood to Manchester, which was discontinued in 2012. The push for its return has been led by Heywood and Middleton MP Elsie Blundell since her election in 2024.

The proposed route would start in Norden, stopping at Bamford, Heywood, and Rhodes before reaching the city centre. Blundell believes that restoring this service would enhance local economic growth and improve transport connectivity for residents.

In a recent House of Commons session, Blundell highlighted that Heywood is the largest town in Greater Manchester without an express bus service to the city centre.

She urged the government to support Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) in delivering this service, which she sees as vital for the community while they await the arrival of Metrolink trams, which are still under consideration.

Burnham criticized the previous Conservative government's decision to deregulate the bus system, stating that it has led to high fares for passengers. He noted that Greater Manchester's public control over buses allows for the introduction of the express service, which he previously supported.

Although current Mayor Bev Craig has not publicly backed the initiative, discussions with Blundell have taken place regarding the express bus and the potential for Metrolink in Heywood.

articles.title: Prohibition of waiting on Manchester Old Road in Middleton from January 2027
articles.excerpt: No waiting will be allowed on part of Manchester Old Road in Middleton from 5 January 2027, affecting local traffic.
articles.content_html:
A prohibition of waiting will be enforced on part of Manchester Old Road in Middleton from 5 January 2027, impacting local traffic flow.

The restriction will be in place from 8am on Tuesday, 5 January until 6pm on Thursday, 7 January 2027.

No waiting will be allowed at any time on the north side of the road, starting 25 metres east of the junction with Chapel Street and extending 33 metres further along.

This decision was made by Rochdale Borough Council to improve traffic management in the area. The council aims to ensure smoother traffic flow and enhance safety for both drivers and pedestrians.

Residents and commuters should be aware of this temporary restriction as it may affect parking and traffic patterns nearby. Further details can be found on the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: Rochdale Council launches Christmas Toy Appeal for local children in need
articles.excerpt: The Christmas Toy Appeal aims to support local children living in poverty by collecting donations until 11 December.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has launched its Christmas Toy Appeal to support local children living in poverty, with donations accepted until Friday 11 December.

The appeal, organised by the charity Number One Riverside Giving Back, aims to provide gifts to children who may otherwise go without this Christmas due to financial pressures faced by their families.

Helen Walton, a council policy advisor from the charity, expressed gratitude for the community's support, stating that every donation is important for the appeal's success and that requests for help have already been received this year.

This initiative is part of a broader effort to alleviate the impact of poverty during the holidays and ensure that children have presents on Christmas Day.

articles.title: Middleton man charged with assaulting emergency worker after Lodge Street stop
articles.excerpt: Lee Cartledge, 42, faces four charges following a vehicle stop in Middleton on Wednesday 11 November, Greater Manchester Police said.
articles.content_html:
A Middleton man has been charged with assaulting an emergency worker following a vehicle stop on Lodge Street in the town on Wednesday 11 November.

Greater Manchester Police named the defendant as Lee Cartledge, 42, of Lawson Close, Middleton.

The force said he has also been charged with possession of a bladed article, driving a motor vehicle without insurance and failing to provide a specimen of breath.

Cartledge is due to appear at Manchester and Salford Magistrates’ Court on Thursday 12 November, according to the police statement issued that morning.

The charges are allegations. No finding of guilt should be inferred, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

Source: Greater Manchester Police press release issued on 12 November 2026.

articles.title: Two Rochdale men among ten charged in drugs supply investigation
articles.excerpt: Two Rochdale men among ten people charged in a Greater Manchester Police drugs investigation were due to appear at Manchester Crown Court today, Friday 13 November.
articles.content_html:
Two Rochdale men among ten people charged in a drugs supply investigation were due to appear at Manchester Crown Court today, Friday 13 November.

Greater Manchester Police named the local defendants as Jailil Ahmed, 53, of Twinegate, Rochdale, and Shakil Ahmed, 51, of Whittaker Lane, Rochdale.

All ten were remanded in custody when they were charged, ahead of the scheduled Crown Court appearance, according to the force. Rochdale Daily has not been able to confirm the outcome of today's hearing.

In a statement issued on 27 October, GMP said eight men, a woman and a 16-year-old boy had been charged with conspiracy to supply controlled drugs in classes A, B and C, and conspiracy to supply an unauthorised medicinal product.

The boy cannot be named for legal reasons. The other adult defendants are from Burnage and Wolverhampton, or have no fixed abode, according to the police statement.

GMP said the charges followed a seven-month investigation by its Serious and Organised Crime Group into suspected large-scale supply and distribution of drugs in Greater Manchester and the West Midlands.

The charges are allegations. No finding of guilt should be inferred, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

Source: Greater Manchester Police press office, press release issued on 27 October 2026.
